strengths: Targets an important and under-explored problem: transparent domain adaptation for clinical EHR prediction, with clear motivation around trust, accountability, and safe deployment.

Combines sparse autoencoders, MMD alignment, and orthogonal residual decomposition into a single framework, and evaluates on two real-world EHR datasets under spatial, temporal, and facility-type shifts.
Provides some theoretical analysis of the dictionary-induced metric, closed-form projection, and projection stability, along with ablation and linear-probe studies.
The qualitative case studies and four-quadrant label/domain sensitivity visualization are clinically intuitive and suggest a useful direction for concept-level auditing.
weaknesses: The evaluation selects the best checkpoint based on target test-set F1 (Appendix I.2), which is test-set leakage and invalidates the unsupervised domain adaptation protocol; reported target performances may be optimistically biased.

The central theoretical claim that domain information concentrates in the residual z while being small in v is inconsistent with the data processing inequality: z is a deterministic function of v (Eq. 7), so I(δ;z) ≤ I(δ;v). If alignment makes I(δ;v) small, z cannot become highly domain-discriminative as claimed.

The interpretation procedure is not faithful to the prediction pathway: the label predictor pζ is applied to v at inference (Sec. 3.5), but the ablation explanations are computed by ablating sparse code s and feeding it to a classifier f_clf (Appendix J.1), without specifying how s relates to the actual prediction.

No quantitative evaluation of transparency/interpretability is provided; evidence is limited to two-patient case studies and qualitative four-quadrant plots, with no faithfulness metric, clinician study, interpretability baseline comparison, or random-dimension control.

The MMD alignment term in Eq. (3) is ambiguous: MMD is defined between distributions, but v_μ and v'_μ appear to be batch means, and the denominator uses ||sg(v_μ)||_F^2; this makes the objective difficult to interpret and reproduce.

Reproducibility is limited: OCHIN is not publicly available, no code link is provided, and there are inconsistencies in the data-split description (e.g., eICU target regions and OCHIN temporal cutoffs differ between main text and appendix).

Baseline adaptations are ad hoc for multi-label diagnosis and HF prediction, with some methods modified or dropped; it is unclear whether baselines were fairly tuned, and ExtraCare does not actually outperform all baselines on all metrics (e.g., eICU HF F1 is higher for BUA).

The paper lacks a limitations section and does not discuss ethical risks, fairness across patient subgroups, or clinical validation, despite motivating the work with health equity and high-stakes clinical deployment.

The theoretical contributions are mostly standard linear algebra/ridge-regression properties; the main adaptation guarantee is an informal remark with unspecified regularity conditions and no formal bound linking orthogonality to target risk.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: making domain adaptation for clinical event prediction transparent, which matters for trust and safety in high-stakes settings.

Uses two real-world, heterogeneous EHR datasets (eICU and OCHIN) and evaluates under multiple domain-shift partitions (spatial, temporal, facility-type), which is more thorough than a single-shift setup.
Combines sparse-autoencoder concept grounding with a disentanglement-style invariant/covariate split, an interesting pairing that could be a useful building block if developed further.
Includes an ablation study isolating the contributions of the reconstruction, orthogonal-residual, and domain-classification components, and reports standard errors across runs.
weaknesses: The central transparency claim is not quantitatively evaluated. Interpretability (RQ2) is supported only by two hand-picked patient case studies (Figure 2) with no faithfulness metric, no comparison to alternative explanation methods, no clinician/user study, and no measure of whether the mapped concepts are correct. For a paper whose headline contribution is transparency, this is a decisive evidential gap.

Potential test-set leakage in model selection: Appendix I.2 states checkpoints are chosen by 'the highest test-set F1 score observed during training.' Selecting the model on the test set optimistically biases every reported number in Tables 2 and 7 and undermines the claimed superiority over baselines.

The claimed 'factorization into invariant and covariant components' is implemented only as a projection along a single direction v̂. The residual z = v − αv̂ separates v from one reconstructed direction, not into two subspaces, and the label predictor p_ζ is trained on the full v rather than on the claimed 'invariant feature.' The framing ('decompose patient representations into two components') substantially overstates what the method actually does.

The interpretation pipeline is internally inconsistent. The classifier is defined to take v (p_ζ(f_φ(x))), but the ablation procedure feeds the ablated sparse vector into a classifier (p̃ = f_clf(s̃)) and recomputes probabilities. It is never explained how manipulating s affects the actual prediction head, which is trained on v, not on s. This raises doubt about whether the attributions reflect the deployed model at all.

The theoretical contributions are thin or overstated. Proposition 1 is a standard weighted least-squares projection, and Lemma 1's stability constant depends on 1/√ε (Eq. 10), so the bound degrades as ε→0 and is essentially a generic Lipschitz statement. The information-theoretic 'Remark' is explicitly informal and the link from MMD ≤ η to I(δ;v) ≲ Cη² is asserted without valid derivation.

Baseline fairness is questionable. RSDA and RCG are stripped of their self-training components 'to ensure a fair comparison,' which can only weaken them, and RCG/CST are dropped for diagnosis prediction. The resulting comparison does not represent the baselines' full published capability.

The domain-induced metric M = W_θ^⊤W_θ is presented as a principled 'dictionary geometry,' but its use is not well motivated: the M-reconstruction loss measures error only in the column space of W, M is degenerate on Null(W_θ), and no evidence shows this geometry is preferable to the Euclidean choice beyond a single ablation row.

Several notation and formulation issues reduce clarity: Eq. (3) mixes CE and MMD under one label, ||sg(v_μ)||_F uses a Frobenius norm on what appears to be a vector, the loss-weight notation (λ_1, λ_2, λ_3 vs λ_label, λ_rec, λ_dcl) is inconsistent, and the SAE latent dimension is stated as 256 = 2d but d is not clearly fixed.

Novelty is incremental: orthogonal invariant/domain-specific disentanglement is well established (e.g., Domain Separation Networks and follow-ups), and the SAE-to-concept mapping is closely adapted from AutoCodeDL. The combination is not shown to yield new understanding beyond modest accuracy gains.

Reproducibility is limited by heavy reliance on an appendix and by the fact that the quantitative interpretability procedure (rank-based domain sensitivity, Δprob threshold) is defined post hoc on a case study rather than as a validated metric.

strengths: Addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: transparent domain adaptation for EHR-based predictive healthcare, with the goal of exposing what is retained vs. removed during adaptation.
Evaluated on two real-world EHR datasets (eICU and OCHIN) under multiple domain-shift settings (spatial, temporal, facility-type), with a broad set of DA baselines and ablations.

The proposed method is conceptually simple and integrates sparse autoencoders, MMD alignment, and orthogonal residual inference; empirical results show consistent improvements over most baselines on diagnosis and heart-failure prediction.

Includes some useful analyses: linear-probe separation of class vs. domain information, ablation of key components, and qualitative case studies linking sparse dimensions to clinically plausible ICD codes.
The paper provides formal statements (closed-form projection, projection stability) and a notation table, which help clarify the geometric construction.
weaknesses: Serious evaluation concern: the paper states that the best checkpoint is selected by 'the highest test-set F1 score observed during training'. In unsupervised domain adaptation, target labels are unavailable; using target test labels for model selection is data leakage and invalidates the claimed unsupervised adaptation comparisons unless this is a typo and target validation data were actually used.

The central claim of decomposing representations into invariant and covariant components is not structurally enforced. The label predictor is trained on v, while z is only the residual v - alpha*v_hat; since v = alpha*v_hat + z, the label predictor can still use z. There is no explicit constraint that z is label-free or that v is domain-free beyond MMD alignment, so the 'functional separation' is heuristic rather than guaranteed.

The information-theoretic remark about domain information concentrating in z is informal and not empirically verified. The paper does not report domain-classifier accuracy on z or quantitative measures of I(delta;z) vs. I(delta;v), so the claimed factorization lacks direct support.

The transparency claim is supported only by qualitative case studies on two patients. There is no quantitative evaluation of explanation faithfulness, concept alignment, stability, or clinician-facing usability, despite 'accurate explanations' and 'enhanced transparency' being central claims.

Theoretical contributions are minor relative to the framing. Proposition 1 is a standard weighted least-squares result, and Lemma 1 is a stability bound for a regularized projection; neither establishes that the method learns invariant/covariant factors or improves target risk beyond existing DA theory.

Experimental setup has inconsistencies and missing details. For example, the main text says eICU target domains are 'West or Midwest', while the appendix says target is only 'Midwest'; dataset statistics (hospital/facility counts) differ between main text and appendix; the training-stage description in Section 3.5 does not fully match the implementation schedule; and the MMD notation in Eq. (3) uses batch means rather than a proper kernel MMD.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data-processing scripts are provided, OCHIN access is restricted, random seeds and number of runs are not reported, and it is unclear whether standard errors are over runs or samples. Hyperparameters are also incompletely specified (e.g., lambda_1 for MMD).

The paper lacks a limitations section and an adequate ethics discussion. The impact statement dismisses societal consequences, and there is no fairness/subgroup analysis despite the stated health-equity motivation; clinical deployment risks, privacy, and potential bias amplification are not addressed.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: transparent domain adaptation for clinical prediction, and proposes a concrete pipeline that links sparse autoencoder concepts to invariant/covariant axes.

Evaluation spans two real-world EHR datasets (eICU, OCHIN), multiple shift settings (spatial, temporal, facility-type), two tasks, and many DA baselines, with ablations and external grounding metrics.

The interpretation pipeline attempts to move beyond post-hoc attribution by training the SAE jointly and using sparse-dimension ablation to categorize concepts into label-impact and domain-sensitivity quadrants.
The manuscript includes useful appendices with pseudocode, hyperparameters, notation, metric properties, and projection-stability analysis, which aids reproducibility.
The external grounding protocol (LAD/DAD/QCE) and paired judge study are a step toward validating explanations against patient relevance and facility specificity.
weaknesses: Critical evaluation flaw: Appendix I.2 states the best checkpoint is selected by highest test-set F1 score, which is target test leakage in an unsupervised DA setting; Appendix I.5 simultaneously says methods are selected on source validation, creating an unresolved contradiction. If test labels are used for checkpointing, the reported DA superiority is not trustworthy.

Inconsistent data split: the main text says eICU target is West or Midwest, while Appendix I.4 says the target is Midwest only and the source includes West. This affects reproducibility and interpretation.

Theoretical support is thin: Proposition 1 is standard weighted least squares; Lemma 1 is a projection-stability bound with a possibly large constant depending on 1/sqrt(epsilon); the information-theoretic Remark is informal and uses gtrsim/lesssim without rigorous assumptions. The overall method's ability to partition domain information is not formally established.

The orthogonal residual construction is essentially a projection onto the SAE reconstruction direction; no proof guarantees that z captures all domain-specific variation while v remains invariant. The domain classifier directly supervises z, but it is not clear why this cannot reintroduce domain information into v through gradients.

Explanation validation is limited: LAD improves from 36% to 47%, DAD only from 40% to 42%, and QCE from 37% to 32%; these are modest gains and no significance tests are reported. The four-quadrant categorization uses an ad hoc threshold and rank-based domain sensitivity.

The concept mapping is not externally validated at the concept level; case studies of two patients and preference judgments by an unspecified LLM and two human evaluators (25 cases) do not establish that sparse dimensions correspond to medical concepts.

Reproducibility and ethics: no code or data-split artifacts are provided; OCHIN data access may be restricted; the human/LLM judge protocol lacks judge identity, qualifications, inter-rater agreement, and data governance/IRB details.

Presentation issues: the notation table is garbled (e.g., the alpha row is misaligned), ablation labels L2/L3 are not clearly defined in the main text, and some claims ('one of the first', 'prevalence-aware') are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and important problem: making domain adaptation for clinical prediction more transparent and interpretable. The motivation around clinician trust and the need to understand what is transferred versus what is removed is well-articulated.

The overall architecture is clearly presented in Figure 1, and the combination of sparse autoencoders with orthogonal decomposition for interpretable domain adaptation is an interesting conceptual direction.
The experimental evaluation is extensive, covering two real-world EHR datasets (eICU and OCHIN) with multiple domain shift scenarios (spatial, temporal, facility-based) and a range of baselines.
The paper includes both quantitative evaluation (LAD, DAD, QCE metrics) and qualitative case studies with clinical interpretation, demonstrating an effort toward rigorous interpretability assessment.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions are flawed and insufficiently supported. Lemma 1 (Stability of M-Orthogonal Projection) appears to have a critical error in the appendix proof: the stated bound uses Π_v^{(M)}(v) in the notation but the derivation only bounds Π_{ν̂}^{(M)}(v) - Π_{ν̂}^{(M)}(v), which is trivially zero. The intended comparison with projection onto v is not actually established, undermining the claimed stability guarantee.

The Remark (Domain Information in z) is explicitly informal and not a rigorous theoretical result, yet it is used to justify a core component of the method. The claimed relations I(δ;z) ≳ 1-h(e_z) and I(δ;v) ≲ Cη² are stated without formal proof or clear assumptions, and the connection between MMD alignment and mutual information reduction is speculative rather than established.

The evaluation of interpretability (RQ2 and RQ3) lacks a rigorous ground truth. The case studies in Figure 2 show that sparse dimensions map to clinically plausible ICD codes, but there is no validation that these explanations are actually correct or that they reflect true model reasoning rather than post-hoc rationalization. The external grounding metrics (LAD, DAD, QCE) compare against patient history and facility prevalence, but these are correlated with the training signal and do not constitute independent validation.

The comparison with SHAP and Integrated Gradients in RQ3 is not methodologically sound. These dense attribution methods operate fundamentally differently from SAE-based sparse explanations, and the comparison after forcing them into the same sparse code budget may not be fair or informative. The paper does not justify why these methods should be expected to separate label and domain axes in the same way.

The human evaluation in Table 3 is insufficient to support the claims. With only 25 cases evaluated by two human raters, the statistical power is very low, and the paper does not report inter-rater reliability or confidence intervals. The LLM judge evaluation (300 cases) is also not a substitute for rigorous human validation.

The method's key innovation—using a domain classifier on the residual z—is not clearly justified theoretically. The paper claims that domain information is 'encouraged' to concentrate in z, but there is no guarantee this actually happens. The ablation results (Table 2) show that removing L_dcl degrades performance, but this could simply mean that any additional supervised signal helps, not that the orthogonal decomposition is working as intended.

The paper does not provide sufficient analysis of whether the orthogonal decomposition actually succeeds in practice. While Table 4 shows cosine similarity between classifier weights, this is a weak proxy for true orthogonality of the underlying representations. There is no direct measurement of whether z actually captures domain-specific variation or whether it contains residual label information.

The interpretation pipeline relies on the prediction head operating directly on the sparse code s, but the inference procedure (Section 3.5) states that predictions are made via p_ζ(f_ϕ(x')). It is unclear how the sparse code is used at inference time, and whether the ablations in Figure 2 are performed on a model that was actually trained end-to-end with the interpretation in mind.

The paper claims 'prevalence-aware interpretation' as a contribution, but this concept is never clearly defined or evaluated. It is not apparent what distinguishes this from standard feature attribution.

The experimental setup has inconsistencies. For example, Table 1 reports eICU as having 9,408 patients and 187 hospitals, but the text in Appendix I.3 states '208 hospitals' and the main text says '208 hospitals across the United States.' These discrepancies raise questions about data preprocessing and reporting accuracy.

The paper does not adequately address potential negative societal impacts or ethical concerns beyond a generic impact statement. Given the clinical application and the focus on fairness across patient populations, a more thorough discussion of potential harms (e.g., perpetuating biases through 'domain-invariant' features that may encode systemic inequities) is warranted.

The reproducibility of the interpretability results is questionable. The paper does not provide sufficient detail on how the sparse dimensions were selected for case studies, how the clinical interpretations were validated, or how the LLM judge was prompted and evaluated. The code and data processing pipeline are not described in enough detail for independent replication.

strengths: Novel integration of sparse autoencoders with domain adaptation for clinical prediction, enabling concept-grounded interpretability that maps latent dimensions to medical concepts.

Strong empirical performance on two large-scale EHR datasets (eICU, OCHIN) across spatial, temporal, and facility-level shifts, often outperforming state-of-the-art DA baselines by significant margins (e.g., 12% relative gain in eICU diagnosis prediction).
Comprehensive evaluation including ablations, external grounding metrics (LAD, DAD, QCE), and human/LLM judge studies, which support the interpretability claims.
Clear and well-organized presentation, with helpful notation table and pseudocode that aid understanding.
Theoretical results (Lemma 1, Proposition 1) provide geometric justification for the orthogonal projection, though they are standard.
weaknesses: Theoretical justification is weak: the lemma and proposition are standard projection properties, and the information-theoretic remark is informal with '≳' and '≲' without rigorous bounds. No generalization guarantee or formal link between orthogonality and improved domain adaptation is provided.

The interpretability evaluation has limitations: the domain sensitivity metric is not rigorously defined (rank-based criterion in Appendix J.1), the external grounding shows only marginal improvement on DAD (40% to 42%), and the human study is small (25 cases, two evaluators with medical training but not necessarily clinicians) and lacks inter-rater reliability.
The strong assumption of covariate shift only (E[y|x] same across domains) is not discussed or relaxed; concept shift could be present in clinical settings, limiting applicability.
No explicit limitations section, and no code release, which hinders reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameters.
The method introduces many hyperparameters (λ1, λ2, λ3, γ, ε, etc.) without sensitivity analysis, except for the threshold τ, making it difficult to assess robustness.
On eICU heart failure F1, ExtraCare (79.64) is slightly worse than BUA (79.83), so the claim of 'superior performance' is slightly overstated.
The term 'prevalence-aware interpretation' is not clearly defined or consistently used, and the interpretation pipeline relies on ad hoc thresholds and rank-based criteria.
